extracted.intended_audience: US citizens or permanent residents applying to the NSF GRFP, especially PhD applicants in CS/NLP/AI/ECE
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for writing NSF GRFP application materials (Graduate Research Plan Statement, Personal Statement, CV, and recommendation letters), targeted to CS/NLP/AI PhD applicants. Emphasizes how reviewers evaluate promise, feasibility, broader impacts, and fit with the applicant's background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the personal element; demonstrate determination and curiosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the personal element of the application and demonstrate a pattern of determination and curiosity about science in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't focus almost entirely on the research proposal at the expense of personal/contextual narrative. The GRFP is designed to nurture promising scientists — show your motivations, persistence, intellectual curiosity, and how your trajectory demonstrates promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate candidate promise over perfect project plans
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the GRFP is to nurture promising scientists, not necessarily to fund the best scientific proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers judge your potential as a scientist. You don't need a flawless or fully executable long-term plan; a well-constructed sample project that shows promise and scientific judgment is sufficient. Aim to meet the program's bar (about 1-in-8 acceptance) rather than 'win' against all peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convincingly address broader impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement needs to convincingly address a real broader impact — how the proposed research will impact society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show understanding of how your research fits public-interest goals of NSF-funded science. Discuss societal benefits concretely and align them with your motivations and proposed activities. Broader impact is tested alongside feasibility and promise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research plan: sketch a coherent, concrete, attainable project grounded in prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: The NSF expects a sketch of a coherent research plan for a couple of years that is concrete and attainable, grounded in your prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a proposal describing what you can most convincingly show you can do right now. Emphasize attainable near-term goals, methods, and how prior experience positions you to achieve them. Reviewers don't expect you to actually carry out the exact project, but they do expect plausibility and grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance accessibility to non-specialists with credibility for experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Your application must be easy to understand for a non-specialist while minimizing the impression of oversimplification for experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thread the needle by writing clearly and avoiding excessive jargon, but include enough substantive detail to avoid being dinged by domain experts. Use layered explanation: high-level motivations and concrete specifics. Ask both in-field and out-of-field readers for feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit feedback from both in-area and out-of-area readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to people in your area as well as not in your area to ensure understandability and to avoid feasibility/ correctness problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-specialists help ensure clarity; specialists catch technical feasibility issues. Getting both perspectives reduces risk of reviewers either not understanding or finding critical technical flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell a story connecting your background to the proposed research
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on telling a story that connects to your demonstrated background and explains why you can do good research in the proposed area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples of past work, skills, and mentorship that prepare you for the proposed project. The narrative should make clear how prior accomplishments lead to the planned research and demonstrate trajectory and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a feasibility paragraph with specifics (data, experiments, training)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a feasibility paragraph discussing where you'll get data, how you'll run experiments, and concrete statements on how your training prepared you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete, executable steps (data sources, methodologies, experimental setups) to show you can realistically perform the proposed work. This strengthens reviewers' confidence in your ability to carry out the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required application components and their roles
rubrics_metrics.description: You must submit a Graduate Research Plan Statement and a Personal/Relevant Background and Future Goals Statement; additionally provide a CV and three letters of recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand each component's purpose: research plan demonstrates project sense/feasibility; personal statement demonstrates background, motivation, and broader impact activities; CV documents accomplishments; letters corroborate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tasteful formatting to highlight key points
rubrics_metrics.description: Use bolding, italicizing, underlining (with taste) to hammer home the few key points from each set of paragraphs and to highlight key definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists read fast; tasteful emphasis helps ensure reviewers notice your main claims. Avoid over-formatting that distracts, but use formatting deliberately to guide quick readers to takeaways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the most appropriate NSF track/discipline strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply in the track that best matches your strengths and experience (e.g., ECE vs CS) because reviewer pools differ and perceived novelty/fit can change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the reviewer audience and how your work will be perceived among that pool. Applying in a discipline where your background and framing stand out positively can help (but be honest about fit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose a project that continues from your demonstrated experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Your proposed project should be a direct continuation of your demonstrated experience; write about what you can convincingly show you can do now, then pivot after award if desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground the research plan in concrete past work rather than speculative leaps; emphasize immediate continuity to reduce perceived risk and increase credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize prior service/outreach and broader impact activities in your background
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer feedback may reward evidence of strong service/outreach and demonstrated broader-impact engagement in your background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document concrete outreach, mentoring, teaching, or community service activities and link them to future broader impact plans to show commitment beyond research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for fast, sometimes superficial panel review; prioritize clarity over perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists tend to read quickly and may breeze through reviews; meeting the program's bar is more important than perfection on every detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity, highlighted takeaways, and meeting core evaluation criteria rather than obsessive polishing. Small errors (e.g., repeated minor misspellings) are unlikely to be fatal if the application clearly demonstrates promise and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sample statements and reviewer feedback resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sample statements from prior applicants and feedback from mentors/previous awardees to inform your application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage networks and publicly shared examples to learn structure, tone, and common pitfalls. Combine samples with personalized feedback to avoid mimicry and to adapt best practices to your story.
